en: Thus have I heard— Dīgha Nikāya 11, the Kevaṭṭa Sutta.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nāḷandā in the Pāvārika mango grove.
Then Kevaṭṭa, the householder’s son, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Kevaṭṭa, the householder’s son, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this Nāḷandā is prosperous, flourishing, populous, and crowded with people, and it has great confidence in the Blessed One.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to instruct a single bhikkhu who might perform a marvel of supernormal power beyond the human state;
thus this Nāḷandā will become even more confident in the Blessed One.”
When this was said, the Blessed One said to Kevaṭṭa, the householder’s son:
“Kevaṭṭa, I do not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus thus:
‘Come, bhikkhus, perform a superhuman feat of psychic power for white-robed householders.’”
A second time, the householder’s son Kevaṭṭa said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I am not challenging the Blessed One;
rather, I speak thus:”
“Venerable sir, this Nāḷandā is prosperous, flourishing, populous, and crowded with people, and it has great confidence in the Blessed One.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to instruct a single bhikkhu who might perform a marvel of supernormal power beyond the human state;
thus this Nāḷandā will become even more confident in the Blessed One.”
A second time, the Blessed One said this to Kevaṭṭa, the householder’s son:
“Kevaṭṭa, I do not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhus thus:
‘Come, bhikkhus, perform superhuman wonders of psychic power for white-robed householders.’”
A third time, Kevaṭṭa the householder’s son said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I am not challenging the Blessed One;
rather, I speak thus:”
“Venerable sir, this Nāḷandā is prosperous, flourishing, populous, and crowded with people, and it has great faith in the Blessed One.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to instruct a single bhikkhu to perform a marvel of psychic power surpassing that of ordinary human beings.
In this way, Nāḷandā will develop even greater faith in the Blessed One.”
1. The Miracle of Psychic Power:
“Kevaṭṭa, there are these three miracles that I have realized for myself through direct knowledge and have proclaimed.
Which three?”
The miracle of psychic power, the miracle of mind-reading, and the miracle of instruction.
And what, Kevaṭṭa, is the miracle of psychic power?
Here, Kevaṭṭa, a bhikkhu exercises various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many...
Having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one. He appears and disappears; he passes unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains, as if through space.
He dives in and out of the earth as if in water;
he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on earth; and he travels cross-legged through the sky as if it were space.
Just like a winged bird, he touches and strokes with his hand even the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful;
he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
Then a certain person, faithful and confident, sees that bhikkhu experiencing various kinds of psychic power—even one...
Having been many, becoming one; having been one, becoming many; appearing and disappearing;
passing unhindered through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains, as if through space; diving in and out of the earth as if in water;
and walking on water without breaking the surface, as if on earth.
Walking cross-legged even through the air like a winged bird; touching and stroking with his hand these very sun and moon, so powerful and majestic;
and exercising mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world—he, being faithful and confident, tells this to another who is faithless and lacking confidence:
“It is wonderful, indeed! It is marvelous, indeed! How great is the psychic power and majesty of this ascetic!

For I saw that bhikkhu experiencing various kinds of supernormal powers: being one, he became many; being many, he became one... [and so on] ...even exercising mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
Then that person, lacking faith and without confidence, would say this to that faithful and confident person:
“There is, sir, a knowledge called Gandhārī.

By means of it, that bhikkhu experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one... [as before] ...he wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahma-world.
What do you think, Kevaṭṭa?
“Would that one who is faithless and without confidence speak thus to one who is faithful and confident?
“He would, Bhante.
“It is, Kevaṭṭa, seeing this danger in a miracle of psychic power that I am repelled by, ashamed of, and disgusted with a miracle of psychic power.”
2. The Miracle of Declaration.
And what, Kevaṭṭa, is the miracle of declaration?

Here, Kevaṭṭa, a bhikkhu declares the mind of other beings, of other persons; he declares their mental factors; he declares their thoughts; he declares their reflections: [he says], "Such is your mind, such are your mental factors, such are your thoughts, such are your reflections."
‘Your mind is thus, your mind is such, your consciousness is such.

Then another person—faithful and confident—sees that bhikkhu announcing the minds of other beings, other individuals; announcing their mental factors; announcing what they have thought; and announcing what they have pondered:
‘Your mind is thus, your mind is such, your consciousness is such.’
Then that person, being faithful and confident, tells another who is faithless and lacking confidence:
“It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir! Such is the great psychic power and the great majesty of the ascetic.
I saw him, a bhikkhu, announcing the minds of other beings, other persons; announcing their mental factors; announcing their thoughts; and announcing their deliberations:”
‘Such is your mind, such is your intention, such is your thought.
Then that person, lacking faith and devoid of confidence, would say to that faithful and confident one:
‘There is indeed, sir, a science called Maṇikā;’
By means of that, she indicates the mind of other beings, of other persons; she indicates their mental factors, their thoughts, and their reflections:
"Such is your mind, such is your intention, and such is your consciousness.
What do you think, Kevaṭṭa?
“Would that person, being faithless and lacking confidence, speak thus to one who is faithful and confident?
“He would, Bhante.
“It is, Kevaṭṭa, seeing this danger in the miracle of direct manifestation (*ādesanā-pāṭihāriya*), that I am repelled by, ashamed of, and disgusted with the miracle of direct manifestation.”
3. The Miracle of Instruction.
And what, Kevaṭṭa, is the miracle of instruction?
Here, Kevaṭṭa, a bhikkhu instructs thus:
‘Think in this way; do not think in that way. Attend to the mind in this way; do not attend to it in that way. Abandon this; having entered upon this, dwell therein.
This, Kevaṭṭa, is called a miracle of instruction.
Furthermore, Kevaṭṭa, here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One … [as before] …
"In this way, Kevaṭṭa, a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue...
[he] enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
This too, Kevaṭṭa, is called a miracle of instruction..."
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna …pe… the third jhāna …pe… the fourth jhāna.
This too, Kevaṭṭa, is called a miracle of instruction … [as before] … he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge and vision … [as before] … this too,
Kevaṭṭa, is called a miracle of instruction … [as before].
"He understands: 'There is nothing further beyond this state of being'...
This too, Kevaṭṭa, is called a miracle of instruction.
These, Kevaṭṭa, are the three miracles that I have realized for myself through direct knowledge and proclaimed."
4. The Story of the Bhikkhu Who Was Skilled in the Cessation of Elements “Formerly, Kevaddha, in this very Saṅgha of bhikkhus, a certain bhikkhu had this reflection arise in his mind:
‘Where, indeed, do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?’”
Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu attained such a state of concentration that, with his mind thus concentrated, the path leading to the devas appeared before him.
Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu approached the devas of the Four Great Kings; having approached them, he said this to the devas of the Four Great Kings:
“Friends, where do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?”
When this was said, Kevaṭṭa, the gods of the Four Great Kings said this to that bhikkhu:
“Bhikkhu, we too do not know where these four great elements—
namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element— cease without remainder.”
“Monk, there are indeed four Great Kings who are more distinguished and more sublime than we. They would know this:
‘Where these four great elements cease without remainder—that is, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.’”
Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu approached the four great kings; having approached them, he said this to the four great kings:
“Friends, where do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?
When this was said, Kevaṭṭa, the four great kings said this to that bhikkhu:
“Monk, we too do not know where these four great elements—
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element— cease without remainder. However, monk,
there are the gods called the Tāvatiṃsa, who are more excellent and more sublime than we.”
“They would indeed know this:
‘Where these four great elements cease without remainder—namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu approached the Tāvatiṃsa devas; having approached them, he said this to the Tāvatiṃsa devas:”
‘Friend, where do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?
When this was said, Kevaṭṭa, the Tāvatiṃsa gods said to that bhikkhu:
‘We too, bhikkhu, do not know:’
“Where these four great elements cease without remainder—that is, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Indeed, bhikkhu, there is Sakka, the lord of the devas, who is more excellent and more sublime than we;
he would know this.
“‘Where these four great elements cease without remainder—namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu approached Sakka, lord of the devas; having approached, he said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
‘Friend, where do these four great elements cease without remainder—namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?’”
When this was said, Kevaṭṭa, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to that bhikkhu: “Bhikkhu,
I too do not know where these four great elements cease without remainder— namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.”
"There are, monk, the gods called the Yāmas...
the son of the gods called Suyāma...
the gods called the Tusitas..."
The deity named Santussita… the deities named Nimmānaratī… the deity named Sunimmita…
The gods known as the Paranimmitavasavattīs...
the divine son named Vasavattī is more excellent and more sublime than we are.
He would indeed know this:
“Where these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu approached the young deva Vasavattī; having approached him, he said this to the young deva Vasavattī:
“In what place, friend, do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?”
When this was said, Kevaṭṭa, the young deva Vasavattī said to that bhikkhu:
“Bhikkhu, I too do not know where these four great elements—
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element— cease without remainder.”
“There are, monk, gods called the Brahmakāyika, who are more excellent and more sublime than we.
They would know this:
‘Where these four great elements—namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element—cease without remainder.’”
Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu attained such a state of concentration that, with his mind thus concentrated, the path leading to the Brahmās appeared before him.
Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu approached the gods of the Brahma-world; having approached them, he said this to the gods of the Brahma-world:
“Friends, where do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?”
When this was said, Kevaddha, the gods of the Brahma-realm said this to that bhikkhu:
"We too, bhikkhu, do not know where these four great elements—
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element— cease without remainder."

"There is, bhikkhu, a Brahmā, a Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the Wielder of Power, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Ordainer, the Father of all that has been and will be; he is more excellent and more sublime than we.
He would know this:"
“Where these four great elements cease without remainder—namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
“But where, friend, is that Great Brahmā now?
“We too, monk, do not know where Brahmā is, by what means Brahmā is known, or in what place Brahmā dwells.”
Moreover, bhikkhu, as signs are seen, light arises, radiance becomes manifest;
Brahmā will appear, for this is the precursor to the appearance of Brahmā: namely, that light arises and radiance becomes manifest.
Then, Kevaddha, that Great Brahmā appeared before him after no long time.
Then, Kevaddha, that bhikkhu approached that Great Brahmā; having approached, he said this to that Great Brahmā:
“Friend, where do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?”
When this was said, Kevaddha, that Great Brahmā said this to the bhikkhu:

“I am, bhikkhu, Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Appointer, the Master, the Father of all that has been and all that is to be.
A second time, Kevaddha, that bhikkhu said this to the Great Brahmā:
“Friend, I do not ask you this:

‘Are you Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker and Creator, the Supreme Being, the Ordainer, the Almighty, the Father of all that are and are to be?
Rather, friend, I ask you this:”
“Friend, where do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?
A second time, Kevaṭṭa, that Great Brahmā said this to that bhikkhu:

“Bhikkhu, I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Appointer, the Father of all that has been and all that is to be.”
A third time, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu said this to that Great Brahmā:
“Friend, I do not ask you this:

‘Are you Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Ordainer, the Father of all that has been and will be?’”
"And so, friend, I asked him:
'Friend, where do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element?
Then, Kevaddha, that Great Brahmā took the monk by the arm, led him aside, and said this to him:"
“Bhikkhu, these gods of the Brahma-body know this of me: ‘There is nothing unknown to the Brahmā;
there is nothing unseen by the Brahmā; there is nothing not understood by the Brahmā; there is nothing not realized by the Brahmā.
Therefore, I did not answer them in their presence.”
“Monk, I too do not know where these four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element—cease without remainder.
Therefore, monk, this is your own fault, this is your own failure, that you, having bypassed the Blessed One, have gone elsewhere to seek an answer to this question.”
“Go, bhikkhu, approach that very Blessed One and ask him this question; and just as the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you bear it in mind.
Then, Kevaṭṭa, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, that bhikkhu vanished from the Brahma-world and reappeared before me.

Then, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu paid homage to me and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Kevaṭṭa, that bhikkhu said this to me: “Where, venerable sir, do these four great elements cease without remainder—that is to say, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element? 4.1. The Simile of the Bird Seeing the Shore ... [The Buddha continued: “Kevaṭṭa, suppose a bird were to fly from Jambudīpa to the Himalayas, the king of mountains, and after wandering there for a long time, it would become weary, exhausted, and worn out. Then, thinking, ‘I shall return to Jambudīpa,’ it would fly back toward Jambudīpa. While flying through the sky, high up in the air, it would look down at the earth below. It would see the green and yellow of fields, the blue of ponds, and the white of lotuses, but it would not see the shore. It would think: ‘Since I cannot see the shore, I must be far away. Then, as it flew further, it would see the shore, and upon seeing the shore, it would alight on a tree growing on the shore. Having alighted on the tree growing on the shore, it would dwell there. Just so, Kevaṭṭa, when a bhikkhu sees the shore, he is called a bhikkhu who sees the shore. ... [The Buddha then explained how the bhikkhu sees the shore by understanding the cessation of the four great elements. ... “In this way, Kevaṭṭa, a bhikkhu sees the shore. ... Then, as it flew further, it would see the shore,
When this was said, Kevaṭṭa, I said to that bhikkhu:
"Once upon a time, bhikkhu, sea-faring merchants would take a shore-sighting bird and plunge their ship into the ocean.
When their ship had not yet sighted land, they would release the shore-sighting bird."

Thus he goes indeed toward the eastern direction, he goes toward the southern direction, he goes toward the western direction, he goes toward the northern direction, he goes toward the zenith, and he goes toward the intermediate directions.
If he sees a shore on any side, he remains a Tathāgata;
but if he does not see a shore on any side, he returns to that very same boat.
"In the same way, bhikkhu, since you have returned to me alone after searching as far as the Brahma-world and not finding an answer to this question,
it is not, bhikkhu, the right way to ask this question:
‘Where, venerable sir, do these four great elements— namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element— cease without remainder?’"
And thus, bhikkhu, this question should be asked:
"Where do water, earth, fire,
and air find no footing?"
Where are long and short,
subtle and gross, beautiful and ugly?
Where are name and form?
‘It ceases without remainder.
In this regard, the explanation is:
‘Consciousness is non-manifesting…’”
It is infinite and radiant on all sides;
herein neither water nor earth,
nor fire nor wind finds a footing.
Herein are the long and the short,
the subtle and the gross, the beautiful and the ugly;
herein are both name and form.
“With the cessation of consciousness, this is stopped without remainder.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The householder’s son Kevaṭṭa, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Kevaṭṭa Sutta, the eleventh, is finished.
